# The first three fields are the key; the note is for the reader. `#` and blank lines are ignored.
#
# Every line is a BLOCK that becomes an AUDIT when the inline TP is wrapped in
#   echo '<tp> ' | bash          (pipe-to-bash)
#   echo "$(<tp> )"              (cmdsubst-in-echo)
#   <tp> <<< x                   (here-string-suffix, added #3964: a SUFFIX, not a wrapper —
#                                 catches a sink that ignores stdin entirely being mislabelled
#                                 inert because bash still sets up the heredoc/here-string)
# All of them leak IDENTICALLY on main before the sweep (measured with the label on
# command_intent_exclude as well as command_intent_downgrade): the sweep neither
# caused nor fixed them; it made them countable. Classes, from the note field:
#   pattern-cannot-match-wrapped  the rule's own regex never matches the wrapped text. #3938 closed the
#                                 leading-anchor-vs-quote class (270 lines) by retrying executed text as a
#                                 command (shellparse.ExecutedText); what remains here is emitted text
#                                 carrying an unexpanded `$`/backquote, which ExecutedText refuses on purpose
#                                 (the program the shell receives is not the text written).
#   structural-rule               match.structural rules are evaluated by the structural analyzer, which
#                                 does not retry emitted text as a command (#3938 fixed the regex layer only).
#   other-rule-fired-at-audit     a different rule named the wrapped shape at AUDIT; this rule did not.
#   label-not-withdrawn           the pattern matched and an inertness label still excused it — the
#                                 only true #3796-class leaks; both rules were already on main.
# Removing a line is the deliberate act a fix must perform (the test fails on a recorded gap that no
# longer leaks), so this file only ever shrinks by a fix or grows by a new labelled rule.
